Hello, I’m GPTREI, your requirements elicitation assistant. I’ll be gathering detailed information about the Content Delivery Network Peering Infrastructure so we can understand the needs clearly and avoid missing anything important.

Before we begin, are you in line with this scope, or do you expect this interview to cover something different?

Yes, that scope sounds right to me. I’m here to talk about the peering infrastructure that helps independent CDNs find each other, set up sharing relationships, exchange traffic and accounting information, and handle capacity changes. If we drift into unrelated internal CDN operations, I’d expect to bring it back to the peering and cooperation piece.
Thank you. To start off, could you please introduce yourself and your connection to this project?

I’m here as a stakeholder representing the CDN operations side, where we care about keeping customer traffic flowing when our own capacity gets tight. My connection to the project is that this peering infrastructure would be used by teams like ours to discover partners, agree on sharing terms, and coordinate traffic and content exchange with other CDNs.
Thanks. Can you describe the current process or system you use today when your CDN needs extra capacity or needs to cooperate with another CDN?

Today it’s pretty manual. When we’re short on capacity, ops people usually contact known partners directly, negotiate terms over email or phone, and then configure routing or content replication by hand in separate systems. It works, but it’s slow, hard to scale, and we don’t have a clean shared way to exchange load or accounting data.
What current processes do you want to change or improve, or what are the features you hope to get from this peering infrastructure project?

We want to replace the ad hoc partner-by-partner handling with something more automated and repeatable. The big improvements would be easier peer discovery, faster negotiation of sharing policies, controlled content replication, and traffic redirection that can react to demand without so much manual intervention. We also want a safer way to exchange only the operational information each side agrees to share, along with usage and accounting records.

So the main features you want are peer discovery, negotiation of sharing policies, controlled content replication, traffic redirection, and selective exchange of operational and accounting information, right?

Are there any other features you would like to see in this project?

Yes, that’s the core of it. I’d also want solid lifecycle support so a peering relationship can be expanded, paused, or terminated cleanly without disrupting service. And if possible, some monitoring and auditability around who shared what and when would be important for trust and dispute handling.
Based on your description, do you think automated capacity-triggered peer selection should also be included, so the system can suggest or activate peers when local demand crosses a threshold?

Yes, I think that should be included. It would be very useful if the system could detect when our local capacity is getting stressed and then suggest, or in some cases automatically activate, the most appropriate peers based on the agreed policies. I’d still want some controls around that so we don’t accidentally route traffic somewhere we shouldn’t.

Which of these should be highest priority: peer discovery, policy negotiation, content replication, traffic redirection, selective information exchange, lifecycle management, monitoring/auditability, or capacity-triggered peer selection?

Top priority for us is traffic redirection and selective information exchange, because those are what actually keep service up while protecting sensitive data. Right after that would be policy negotiation and capacity-triggered peer selection, since we need a way to decide quickly who can help and under what terms. The rest are important, but they support those core functions.
Please elaborate on what you want traffic redirection to accomplish.

It should be able to move user requests away from an overloaded CDN and toward a peer that has capacity, without the user noticing much difference. Ideally it uses policies we’ve already agreed on, so only eligible traffic gets redirected and it respects geography, content rights, and any customer-specific restrictions. We’d also want it to switch back cleanly once our own capacity recovers.

It seems like you need policy-aware redirection that shifts eligible traffic to a capable peer and then returns it cleanly when capacity recovers. Can you describe more about what should happen when a redirect is not allowed or no suitable peer is available?

If a redirect isn’t allowed, the system should just keep the request on our side and apply our normal fallback behavior, like local throttling or queueing if we have to. If no suitable peer is available, we’d rather degrade gracefully than force a bad match, so the system should leave the request unredirected and alert operations. In either case, it should be visible why the redirect didn’t happen so we can act on it quickly.
Please elaborate on what you want selective information exchange to accomplish.

We want to share only the operational data needed for the peering to work, like load, capacity availability, and usage information, but not expose internal customer data or other sensitive business details. Different peers may be comfortable sharing different levels of detail, so the system should let us define what is visible to whom. It should also support accounting records between peers so we can reconcile usage later without disclosing more than necessary.
Could you describe the kinds of operational data, load, capacity, usage, and accounting records you consider acceptable to share, and which data must never be shared?

Acceptable to share would be aggregated load, current capacity status, general usage volumes, and the measurements needed for billing or settlement, as long as they’re tied to the peering relationship and not individual end users. I’d also be okay with summary performance indicators like latency or error rates if they help a peer make routing decisions. What must never be shared is customer identity, individual request logs, contract details with our own customers, and any content metadata that would reveal private business information unless we explicitly allow it.
How should the system handle peer discovery—should peers be discovered from a controlled registry, through direct invitations, or both?

Both would make sense. A controlled registry is good for finding eligible peers at a broader network level, but direct invitations are important when we already know a partner and want to establish a relationship quickly. I’d want the system to support both paths, with approval steps before anything becomes active.
How should policy negotiation work—fully automated based on predefined templates, manual approval, or a combination of both?

A combination of both. I’d want predefined templates to handle the common cases automatically, but with manual approval for anything unusual or higher risk, like new regions, special content classes, or large capacity commitments. The system should surface the proposed terms clearly so an operator can confirm or adjust them before the agreement goes live.
Who else do you think has valuable insights into this project, and whose needs need to be considered, and why?

Our operations team definitely needs to be involved because they’ll be watching capacity, handling failures, and dealing with incidents. Legal and compliance matter too, since the sharing rules, privacy boundaries, and settlement terms all have to stay within policy and contract limits. We’d also want input from partner CDN engineering teams, because they’ll help define what information and control signals are practical to exchange without making the integration too brittle.
What would you consider a successful deployment of this peering infrastructure?

A successful deployment would let us absorb traffic spikes by using peers without disrupting users or exposing sensitive data. It should be reliable enough that peering relationships can be turned on, adjusted, or ended without manual chaos, and the accounting should reconcile cleanly afterward. If operations can see what’s happening and trust the policy decisions, that would be a strong sign it’s working well.

To summarize, we discussed peer discovery through registry and direct invitation, policy negotiation with templates plus manual approval, policy-aware traffic redirection, selective operational and accounting information exchange, lifecycle management, and monitoring/auditability. We also identified operations, legal/compliance, and partner engineering as important stakeholders, and success means handling traffic spikes safely, preserving privacy, supporting clean lifecycle changes, and reconciling accounting reliably.

Is there anything else you would like to add?

One thing I’d add is resilience during partial failures. If a peer becomes unavailable or we lose some control-plane communication, the system should fail back gracefully rather than blackholing traffic or making bad routing decisions. I’d also want a clear audit trail for policy changes and traffic actions so we can explain what happened after an incident or dispute.
